title: Universal crosses the finish line with a new world-class coaster
summary:
By Robert Niles: Let�s talk about drifting.

In auto racing, there are few more spectacular sights that watching cars burn through a turn at high speed, wheels smoking, as drivers balance on the edge of control. A race car drifting through a turn does not drive parallel to the edges of the track like a responsible drivers ed graduate trying to pass their test at the DMV. Instead, pro racers slide through the turn at absurd angles, pushing their car sideways against its momentum.

It�s all because of the lesson that Doc Hudson taught Lightning McQueen in the original "Cars." Sometimes, you have to turn right to go left. As you mash that accelerator and hold it down through a turn, a car�s natural reaction is for that rear end to snap around, turning faster than the front. To counter that, you pick just the right moment to twist the wheel the opposite way, turning into the skid.

If you took the corner at high enough speed, the conflict between the direction of the front and rear wheels will resolve into an angry compromise, as the car slides, or drifts, through the turn at maximum speed. When it happens, the tires are no longer driving the car as much as they are being dragged along for the ride, creating those thrilling pillars of smoke.

Of course, dragging that handbrake or shifting just right for some extra wheel spin can help amplify the smoke and sound. From street races and takeovers to the professional ranks of the Formula Drift circuit, drifting captures eyeballs as well as checkered flags, making a ride in a drifting racecar a wish fulfillment moment for many race fans.

Which brings us to Universal Studios Hollywood�s new roller coaster, Fast & Furious Hollywood Drift. Namechecking the third movie in the franchise, "Fast & Furious: Tokyo Drift," this new thrill ride from Intamin and Universal Creative promises riders Universal's fastest roller coaster in the world, with a top speed of 72 mph.

But this is not Universal's first attempt at a Fast & Furious ride. Let's talk about another meaning of that word, "drift." Because when I think of drifting and Fast & Furious, I also think about how this franchise has drifted over the years from gritty films about street racing to absurdist, CGI-driven heist fantasies that defy every law of physics, economics, and Hollywood star management.

Universal got caught in that Hollywood Drift with its Fast & Furious Supercharged attraction, which delivered moments that exactly zero fans ever wished for � to sit on a bus and watch grainy Pepper�s Ghost images of Fast & Furious stars before lumbering into yet another Universal 3D CGI screen attraction. Now that experience is gone on both coasts, and let us never speak of it again.

In its place now, we have Fast & Furious Hollywood Drift, which opens officially to USH visitors Wednesday. On the east coast, Universal Studios Florida fans can anticipate getting their own version of the coaster sometime in the spring (maybe?) next year.

I was out of town when Universal first soft-opened the ride last month, so I chose to wait for my first run today, when the park hosted its media preview. Universal had invited me to check out the ride�s cars, station and track before opening it to the public, so I was not walking into this experience cold.

But even though I knew what this track looked like, I still wondered, how would it feel to ride? Universal and Intamin have created a unique system for spinning these muscle car-themed vehicles on the track. They do not spin randomly or via weight distribution, like so many other spinning coasters. Instead, Universal Creative team has choreographed these cars in an attempt to find just the right balance between thrill and comfort for the millions of fans who visit the park each year.

To me, that challenge sounded a bit too much like the "you have to turn right to go left" riddle that left Lightning McQueen so confused. A real drifting race car pulls unimaginable lateral G forces. And hard lateral G�s often are riders' least favorite feeling on a coaster. How can Universal make a drifting street racer roller coaster that won�t leave riders feeling like they�ve just been in a high speed wreck?

It turns out, the answer is right there in the coaster�s name. It�s a "Hollywood" drift � it�s all make believe.

The dominant feeling on Fast & Furious Hollywood Drift is not lateral G force. It�s hangtime. You will spend as much time out of your seat on this coaster as race fans do watching a last lap battle for the lead at the Indianapolis 500. The spinning on Hollywood Drift feels more like gentle turns, like an Omnimover swiveling to adjust your point of view on a dark ride.

Disney explored a similar ride system with its Guardians of the Galaxy Cosmic Rewind at Walt Disney World�s EPCOT. But Disney�s supposed "family" coaster pulls a much more intense lateral G moment than anything on Hollywood Drift, which has a 51-inch height requirement.

I spoke with Universal Creative's Jon Corfino, who talked me through the ride and Universal�s approach to creating it.

Out of the station, Hollywood Drift makes coy turn to its left as it drops slightly into its first maneuver. Like skillful racer�s move, it�s just a set-up for the more aggressive cornering to come. Let Corfino explain it:

"You go into a deep left bank down, where you can't see where you're going, into what we call a hopper, where you pull your first negative G. Then you're going into the pretzel, where you're doing a couple inversions, and then accelerating down into the loop down by the film building. That's when you hit the big launch, when you go 72 miles an hour, and then you go inverted."

From there, the coaster hangs over then slides under the Starway on its way back to the station. Hops of airtime set up many of the inversions, which make great use of the hangtime that Universal perfected on its Jurassic World VelociCoaster in Orlando.

All that said, it�s Coaster 101 at this point that the back seat of any coaster offers a more intense physical experience, given the pull over track elements from the back of the train. Somehow, with the differing spinning on each car, Universal has managed to amplify that effect, with the Toyota Supra in the back pulling a much more forceful run through Hollywood Drift�s elements than the Dodge Charger up front.

More time up front means more endurance for re-rides, for me, at least. What does not seem to matter as much on this coaster is the view. Joe Rohde has a great scientific explanation for this in this week's Theme Park Insider Podcast, which drops Thursday morning. Science teaches, Rohde said, that our vision constricts as we move faster. So as Hollywood Drift speeds up, we tune out its amazing views of the San Fernando Valley and the mountains surrounding it as we focus on the track ahead� and sometimes, people staring back at us from the car that we though was behind us just a moment ago.

But that�s the nature of a street race, isn�t it? Who is ahead at one moment might not be ahead in the next. Ultimately, as another car-themed attraction down the 5 taught us, the race itself does not matter. We all win, because we all got to go on this ride.

Sum it up, and Hollywood Drift delivers the wish fulfillment of being in the passenger seat for a thrilling, high-speed race. This is the Fast & Furious attraction that fans of the "family" have deserved and have been awaiting for the past 25 years. It's the perfect setting for the world-class, iconic coaster that Universal Studios Hollywood has lacked.

Update: The stars did not show for Universal's media opening moment this evening.

Universal had promoted to invited media that Vin Diesel would be on hand to open officially Universal Studios Hollywood's new coaster. But the Fast & Furious star and producer no-showed for the ceremony. As did other invited stars of the franchise.

Awkward. But the show did go on, though just with USH EVP and GM Scott Strobl and Universal Destinations & Experiences Chairman and COO Mark Woodbury. Despite Universal holding this event the day after the Emmys, when every celebrity is in town and nothing is in production. title: Rohde, Weis, Iwerks set for IAAPA Legends panel
summary:
By Robert Niles: Former Walt Disney Imagineers Joe Rohde and Bob Weis will join documentarian Leslie Iwerks for Bob Rogers' annual Legends panel at the IAAPA Expo this November.

This is the 24th year for Rogers' meeting of the minds of the themed entertainment design industry. The 90-minute panel gathers some of the most accomplished designers and leaders in the theme park industry to share stories and lessons from their careers. This year's Legends panel will happen at 4pm on November 18 at the IAAPA Expo in Orlando, Florida.

All three of this year's panelists have new projects out, including Iwerks' Disney Worldbuilders and Disneyland Handcrafted, with a new season of The Imagineering Story in production. Rohde just published his first book, "Floating Mountains," which we will be featuring on the Theme Park Insider Podcast this week, when Joe joins us as our guest.

Weis also recently published his memoir, "Dream Chasing," as well as his first novel, "Ghost Dog." Rogers himself also has his first book out, "Deep Story," which we featured on the podcast a couple weeks ago.

Rogers will have a second presentation earlier in the week at IAPA, where he talks about his new book in conversation with Weis. That will happen on Monday, November 16 at 10am. For more on the Expo, visit IAAPA.org.

title: Walt Disney World tests new, simpler way to book vacations
summary:
By Robert Niles: Walt Disney World is testing a new way for families and fans to book their theme park vacations.

The resort has redesigned its website and now select users are seeing a beta test for a "Guided Search" option on the DisneyWorld.com home page. Visitors who select that option will be able to browse rates by season as well as dates and can use a newly improved chat and a comparison tool to help them decide what package to book.


If you do not see the "Guided Search" option, you don't have the new version of the site. All images are courtesy Disney

Disney has partnered Google Cloud for AI-powered pattern matching and natural language search functions to help drive the new vacation booking engine for website users. The beta test is limited to randomly selected website users from the United States and Canada. Disney's plans is to expand the functionality in phases.

The AI that Disney is using is not generative AI "trained" on (ahem, I mean, plagiarizing from - yeah, I said it) online sources. Instead, it is using Disney's own database of information about its resorts, rates, and availability to connect website users with what the system determines is the most relevant information for what the user is looking for. It's a more direct and automated approach than the current method of publishing that information into FAQ answer webpages and directing internal website requests to them for guests to read.


The new, natural language search page

In addition, the new system enables Disney to support resort-by-resort comparisons for vacation package options, as well as to allow more options for browsing alternatives, including browsing by season and event.


A new price comparison page

Disney recently redesigned its homepage online for all users, reducing the number of links on the page. It also has introduced Spanish language support on the Walt Disney World and Disneyland apps, as Disney works to improve its guest-facing information technology.

Of course, if you want to skip all the website stuff and just leave your vacation booking to a professional, you may continue to do that. (For assistance in planning a Walt Disney World vacation, please contact our travel agent for a free, no-obligation vacation quote.)

title: Universal Orlando welcomes new celebrity hot dog stand
summary:
By Robert Niles: CityWalk's new celebrity hot dog stand opens this weekend in Orlando.

Universal Orlando has announced a Saturday grand opening for Fat One's Hot Dogs & Italian Ice, which takes over the former Hot Dog Hall of Fame space on CityWalk.

Founded by *Nsync member Joey Fatone, Fat One's previously had a location at the Florida Mall. The CityWalk location will feature a menu of nine topped hot dogs, including the eponymous The Fat One, a footlong hot dog topped with roasted pork, pepperoni, chili beans, cheddar cheese sauce, red onion sauce, pop fries, and chives.

The first 100 guests in line on Saturday morning will get a free hot dog served by Fatone himself.

Also on Saturday, Universal Orlando CityWalk will celebrate the 10th anniversary of The Toothsome Chocolate Emporium & Savory Feast Kitchen from 3-6pm, with an interactive chocolate dipping station and a Toothsome 10th Anniversary Milkshake available for purchase.

title: Rope Drop: Who's ready for a haunt?
summary:
By Robert Niles: This weekend is the big one for theme park haunt events, with Halloween season taking over parks across the country.

But before the scare actors hit the streets, theme park fans this week will welcome the official debut of the Fast & Furious Hollywood Drift roller coaster at Universal Studios Hollywood on Wednesday. Watch the site Tuesday for coverage of the grand opening celebration and our review of Universal's fastest-ever coaster.

Down the road in Anaheim, it's Gay Days at the Disneyland Resort this week, from September 18 through the 20th.

Now for the Halloween stuff. The industry's original after-hours haunt event returns on Thursday with the debut of 2026's Knott's Scary Farm - so watch for our coverage on Friday. Elsewhere in California, Six Flags Fright Fest kicks off Friday at Magic Mountain, along with Queen Mary's Dark Harbor, Los Angeles Haunted Hayride in Griffith Park, and Festival Fright Nights at Winchester Mystery House up the coast in San Jose. On Saturday, Legoland California starts its Brick-or-Treat, while Six Flags Discovery Kingdom kicks off its Oktoberfest.

Around the country, Cedar Point HalloWeekends starts Thursday, followed by Kings Dominion Halloween Haunt and Six Flags Great Adventure Fright Fest on Friday, and Six Flags Great America Fright Fest on Saturday.

Planning a trip?

title: Walk Time: Happy birthday to Hong Kong Disneyland
summary:
By Robert Niles: In theme parks and entertainment, "walk time" is the name for the final paid minutes of your shift, when you gather your stuff and start heading home. At Theme Park Insider, "Walk Time" is our weekend look back at the past seven days in theme park news.

Happy 21st birthday today to Hong Kong Disneyland, which first opened to guests on September 12, 2005.

Several theme park haunts have opened this weekend, including Hersheypark Dark Nights and Howl-O-Scream at SeaWorld and Busch Gardens parks across the country. If anyone would like to share a trip report from any of these events, we'd love to read it over on the discussion forum.

Six Flags dominated this news this week, with its announcements of the new Thrill Glider coming to Magic Mountain, its purchase of ArieForce One, and a new monthly payment plan for season passes. Jake and I ripped into that last one on the Theme Park Insider Podcast this week.

At Walt Disney World, the resort this week showed off to invited reporters its new The Magic of Disney Animation area at Disney's Hollywood Studios. In case you missed it, here are our stories:

  • Step into The Magic of Disney Animation at Disney World
  • The pre-show is the star in Disney's new studio show
  • Olaf draws a new home for animation at Walt Disney World

Looking ahead, Disney also announced dates for its first two festivals in 2027: The EPCOT International Festival of the Arts will run January 15 - March 1, while the next EPCOT International Flower & Garden Festival will run from March 10 to May 31.

Finally, this week I spoke with the leaders of the team that is bringing The Wizarding World of Harry Potter to Yas Island in Abu Dhabi. The expansion of Warner Bros. World Abu Dhabi is now under construction for an estimated completion in 2029. Find out what Miral CEO Dr. Mohamed Abdalla Al Zaabi and Warner Bros. title: Olaf draws a new home for animation at Walt Disney World
summary:
By myhandsdontscan: Animated storytelling is the foundation of The Walt Disney Company. Animated shorts paved the way for feature animation, a music company, live-action features, television specials, theme parks, cruise lines, and now streaming services. The theme parks may now be Disney�s current cash cow, but animation will always be the cornerstone of its flywheel.

It�s a no-brainer, then, to have animation activities featured in the theme parks to pay tribute to this legacy and inspire the next generation of animators. This manifested at Walt Disney World in the form of Hollywood Studios� Animation Academy (drawing classes led by working Disney Animators), another Animation Academy in DisneyQuest (featuring digital sketch pads), and finally The Animation Experience at Conservation Station (drawing animal characters in Animal Kingdom after hopping aboard the Wildlife Express).

After the revamp of Conservation Station to home �Bluey�s Wild World,� the Walt Disney World parks have been absent an animation experience. That is, until the opening of The Magic of Disney Animation at Disney's Hollywood Studios.

This new experience marries both foundational components, animation and storytelling, of the studio that was �all started by a Mouse.�

But in this case it all starts with a snowman.


Entrance to �Olaf Draws!�

�Olaf Draws!� is the new interactive sketching show inside The Magic of Disney Animation. In this experience guests learn, alongside a wonderfully devious animatronic Olaf (who has seemingly taken over the Animation Academy), how to draw a Disney character from a rotating selection of 9 different artists from the studio�many of them drawing characters they helped create.

The list of available characters and their respective animators are:

  • Mickey Mouse, with Dan Abraham
  • Minnie Mouse, with Hyun Min Lee
  • Donald Duck, with Austin Traylor
  • Genie, with Eric Goldberg
  • Moana, with Samantha Vilfort
  • Stitch, with Fawn Veerasunthorn
  • Olaf, with Trent Correy
  • Ursula, with Michael Woodside
  • Judy Hopps & Nick Wilde, with Byron Howard

Guests are seated in spacious animators� desks and are provided sturdy pages of drawing paper and cups full of sketching pencils. Screens are set up around the desks, making it easy to follow along with the animators in their pre-recorded interactions.


The auditorium of �Olaf Draws!�

When the show starts, the animatronic Olaf comes to life and shortly begins interacting with one of the animators. This is a great animatronic with fluid and expressive movements, a nice �plus-up� from what could have been an otherwise screen-guided experience.

Throughout the instruction Olaf and the animator exchange delightful barbs (this is Josh Gad at his unhinged best), adding a bit of levity and chance for some of the slower drawers in the audience (me) to catch up. I found Olaf funny without being annoying or overused.

Each session lasts around 11 minutes, and I found it pretty easy to follow along for most characters. Though I will admit the speed with some of the more involved characters like Genie was a bit fast for an artistically challenged person who struggles to draw stick figures and abstract art. But it was nevertheless enjoyable. And the animators must know what they�re doing because my sketches actually turned out looking like something resembling the characters. We were even given a mailing tube afterwards for keeping our sketches safe.


I offer Eric Goldberg my sincerest apologies.

But it�s in the moments of pause where the show really shines. The animators get a chance to talk about what inspired them to get into animation or why a certain character resonates with them. They aren�t just teaching you how to draw Mickey Mouse, they�re telling a story about why Mickey Mouse is so resonant.

It�s these personal stories from the animators that justify the pre-recordings. Sure, live animators can provide live feedback, but there�s something remarkable about watching Eric Goldberg draw The Genie (and go toe-to-toe with Olaf to boot). By all means mourn the loss of live animators in the parks, but Disney was able to create a wholly new experience that weaves together animation and storytelling in a seamless experience.

And that�s worth melting for.

�Olaf Draws!� opens with The Art of Disney Animation September 14. Virtual waitlists may be used as needed.

title: The pre-show is the star in Disney's new studio show
summary:
By myhandsdontscan: How do you create an engaging attraction from an animated short guests can watch anytime on Disney+? You make it come alive.

Once Upon A Studio, the Emmy-award winning animated short celebrating 100 years of Disney Animation, was used as inspiration for The Magic of Disney Animation area at Hollywood Studios. Animated characters hop out of their films and drawings and into our world.

That same principle applies to this screening of Once Upon a Studio. The short plays inside a dedicated theater within The Magic of Disney Animation. During portions of the film, animated portraits on both sides of the screen come to life, rushing to be in Mickey�s group photo, adding an extra layer of interaction as well as easter eggs for the repeat viewers to spot.

Once Upon A Studio is worthy of its praise � it hits all the emotional and comedic beats without any fat to trim. But the real treat is actually in the pre-show.

Here, portraits of characters come to life on the wall with PhotoPass opportunities and interactive games. Guests can inflate balloons with Baymax or rock the boat with the Kakamora from �Moana.� After completing the tasks, guests can then strike a pose and get a picture taken with the animated characters. The games also have an element of replay-ability with a scoring system.

This pre-show room will surely be a hit for kids � the waiting doesn�t feel like waiting, and if you�ve already seen Once Upon A Studio, it might be better than the theater experience itself.

Once Upon A Studio will offer guests the perfect gateway to The Magic of Disney Animation experience, which opens September 14.
